chapter_theme: Under the heading பொருளைப் பெறுதல், eight verses on keeping wealth rather than winning it: look ahead to one's own wealth and kin's, guard it oneself and not through untested kin, the base or the man of no family, keep it in a fit place, do not neglect it and hope to recover it later, and know that wealth let go or lent out does not come back without anger.

205.reading: The verse urges looking ahead to one's own wealth and to the prosperity of one's kin and taking care to sustain them, and proves it with the proverb of the snail that took in water having looked to the distance.
205.nuance: The care is double: one's own goods and the வளமை of one's kin are both to be looked to முந்துற, beforehand. The proverb is read here as the snail that keeps water in its shell against the dry time; சேணோக்கி may also mean looking far off in space, and நந்து can mean 'increase', so the image is not certain.

pazhamozhi.literal: like the snail that took in water

story.act: no story; the proverb's snail, having looked ahead, holds water for the time to come

pazhamozhi.applied_to: providing in advance for one's own wealth and one's kin's

206.reading: Unless one guards one's own goods without ever forgetting them, the wise do not put them in the hands of those they have not tested, on the ground that they are eminent or are kin, for no one knows how to bring back what is gone.
206.nuance: சிறந்தார் தமர் என்று names the two pretexts for trust, standing and kinship, and the verse sets both aside in favour of testing (தேற்றார், those not made sure of). The proverb makes the loss final rather than merely likely.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one who knows how to bring back what has passed away

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to wealth handed to untested kin and lost

pazhamozhi.applied_to: kinship and standing are no ground for entrusting wealth without testing

207.reading: Precious wealth kept in an unfit place is not saved even by guarding it without blinking, since even the unblinking gods, guarding their nectar at that time, had it carried off; so a hard enclosure is better than good watching.
207.nuance: The verse puns on இமையாது, 'without blinking', and இமையோர், the gods who never blink: the most vigilant guards there are still lost the nectar. The proverb ranks the place over the watcher. The verse names neither the thief nor the episode.

pazhamozhi.literal: a harsh enclosure is better than a good guard

story.act: the gods guarded the nectar and still had it taken from them
story.tradition: by tradition Garuda's carrying off of the nectar; the verse does not name him

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a secure place keeps wealth where vigilance alone does not

208.reading: Handing over the bright wealth one earned by striving and toil to worthless men with a careless 'look after it' is like rice put in a crow's keeping.
208.nuance: இகழ்ந்து marks the fault as the owner's contempt for his own labour, not only the keeper's baseness; ஊக்கி உழந்து sets the effort of earning against the ease of the handing over. நொள்வியார் is a rare form; the proverb makes the sense, unfit keepers, clear.

pazhamozhi.literal: rice put in the crow's keeping

story.act: no story; the keeper set over the rice is the one who eats it

pazhamozhi.applied_to: wealth entrusted to the base is consumed by the very keeper

209.reading: Placing gathered wealth in the hands of a man who is not of a good family is, the verse tells a woman, grass fed to a sluggish ox.
209.nuance: குடிமகன் அல்லான் makes birth the test of a keeper, where 208 made worth the test. மூரி is read as an ox that will not work: the grass is spent and nothing comes of it, so the loss is waste, not theft. The address to a woman is the verse's frame, not its audience.

pazhamozhi.literal: grass fed to a sluggish ox

story.act: no story; the feed is spent on a beast that gives no work

pazhamozhi.applied_to: wealth entrusted to a man of no family is spent without return

210.reading: Neglecting what one had at first and then later trying to search it out and get it back is, the verse says, the way of catching a peacock by putting butter on its head.
210.nuance: The proverb is of a roundabout trick that cannot work: the bird is gone before the butter melts. The verse does not say recovery is impossible, as 206 does, but that the late effort is absurd beside the early guarding it replaces.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way of catching a peacock by setting butter on it

story.act: no story; the proverb is a fool's method of catching a bird

pazhamozhi.applied_to: recovering neglected wealth afterwards is a futile roundabout effort

211.reading: Those who say that bright wealth once let out of hand does not come back are those who have learned it as it truly happened, for, as the proverb says, he who got the loan got the pot.
211.nuance: மெய்ப்பட்ட வாறே உணர்ந்தார் grounds the saying in experience, not precept. The proverb is obscure: கடம் may be a debt or a large pot, and the line seems to say that whoever has received the thing holds it. The reading here takes கடம் as the loan.

pazhamozhi.literal: he who got the loan (or the jar) got the pot

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to wealth that has passed into another's hand

pazhamozhi.applied_to: wealth let go belongs in effect to whoever now holds it

212.reading: When those who have lent out bright wealth and let it lie then take their moment and say 'give it to us', the borrowers turn on them as if they had taken up a feud, and the anger of those who took turns even past good cheer into bitterness.
212.nuance: The fault lies on both sides: the lender let the loan lie (கைவிட்டிருப்பார), and the borrower answers a just claim with enmity. நகைமேலும் suggests the friendly ease that made the loan possible is what turns bitter.

pazhamozhi.literal: the anger of those who took turns bitter even over laughter

story.act: no story; the borrower asked to repay grows angry

pazhamozhi.applied_to: asking back a loan left long unclaimed turns the borrower into an enemy

links.note: Kural 429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming are not shaken by affliction; Pazhamozhi 205 applies that foresight to one's own wealth and to the prosperity of one's kin.
links.teaches: The Kural's foresight is a general shield against calamity; the snail that stores water shows it as stockpiling for a known dry season, so foresight becomes provision for kin as well as self.
links.list_adds: it joins one's own wealth and the kin's prosperity as one object of forethought, which the couplet leaves unnamed, and gives the snail as the instance.

links.note: Kural 508 warns that trusting an outsider (பிறன்) without examining him brings lasting trouble; Pazhamozhi 206 refuses even eminent men and kin the trust of one's goods until they are tested.
links.teaches: The Kural's danger is the untested stranger; Pazhamozhi removes the exemption kinship might seem to give, so testing applies inside the family too, and adds that the loss of entrusted wealth cannot be reversed.
links.list_adds: it names the two pretexts for trust, standing and kinship, and sets both aside, which the couplet does not, since it speaks only of the outsider.

links.note: Both speak of guarding ஈட்டிய ஒண்பொருள், earned bright wealth: the Naladiyar calls that guarding bitter suffering and wealth the dwelling of suffering, while Pazhamozhi 208 counts guarding it oneself a duty and handing it carelessly to others a folly.
links.teaches: On the same phrase the Jain quatrain makes custody of earned wealth a burden to be shed, by giving it away, while Pazhamozhi makes it a charge never to be delegated, so the two disagree on whether keeping earned wealth is worth its care.
links.list_adds: its crow proverb makes the careless handing over the fault, where the quatrain's list of sufferings makes the guarding itself the fault.

links.note: Both use grass fed to a bullock that will not work: the Naladiyar's small bullocks never take the yoke however much cut grass they eat, and Pazhamozhi 209's grass is fed to a sluggish ox.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar uses the ox to show that the base cannot be improved by feeding, while Pazhamozhi uses it to show the feeder's loss, so the one image condemns the base man's nature in one book and the owner's choice of keeper in the other.
links.list_adds: it moves the image from the base man who has come into wealth to the wealth a householder hands to a man of no family, making the image a counsel on custody.

links.note: Kural 1000 says great wealth got by a man without courtesy spoils like good milk in a faulty vessel; Pazhamozhi 209 says wealth placed in the hands of a man not of good family is grass fed to a sluggish ox.
links.teaches: The Kural blames the holder's character for spoiling his own wealth, while Pazhamozhi turns this into a rule for the owner who chooses a keeper, and makes birth rather than courtesy the test.
links.list_adds: it carries the couplet's claim from the man who owns wealth to the man to whom wealth is entrusted, and its proverb makes the loss a waste with no return rather than a spoiling.

links.note: Kural 535 says the man who slipped by not guarding beforehand grieves afterwards over his own error; Pazhamozhi 210 says neglecting what one had and searching to get it back later is catching a peacock with butter.
links.teaches: The Kural leaves the negligent man with regret, while Pazhamozhi follows him into his attempt to undo the loss and shows the attempt itself as absurd, so the cost of neglect is wasted effort as well as grief.
links.list_adds: its proverb mocks the method of recovery, a stage the couplet does not reach, and fixes the neglect on wealth one already had.

links.note: 206 bars entrusting wealth to untested kin and eminent men; 208 bars handing it carelessly to worthless men; both turn on wealth put into another's hands.
links.teaches: Read together, the two verses show the danger of entrusting wealth from both sides: the keeper may be untested though respectable, or plainly base, and in each case the owner's own lapse is the fault.

links.note: 211 says wealth let out of hand does not come back; 212 says a lender who let a loan lie and then asks for it is met with the borrower's anger.
links.teaches: 212 supplies the mechanism behind 211's maxim: lent wealth fails to return not only by loss but because asking for it turns the borrower hostile, so the loan costs the friendship as well as the goods.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 9 says a debtor's tongue dies when he once sees his creditor; Pazhamozhi 212 says the borrower asked to repay grows angry as if at an enemy.
links.teaches: The Sirupanchamoolam gives the debtor's shame and Pazhamozhi his anger, and Pazhamozhi ties the anger to the lender's long delay, so shame is seen to turn into resentment once a loan has lain unclaimed.

source_issues: 208: நொள்வியார் is a rare or possibly corrupt form; the sense, unfit keepers, rests on the proverb.
211: the proverb கடம்பெற்றான் பெற்றான் குடம் is obscure; கடம் may be a debt or a pot.
212: the opening quotation mark falls mid-line 3, so the proverb as printed includes கொண்டார் வெகுடல், which also completes the counsel's clause.
